evals.name: goroutine-lifecycle-proof-without-mandatory-tool
evals.description: Tests use goleak for goroutine leak detection, not just task completion
evals.prompt: Write tests for a workerpool package exposing Start, Submit, and Stop. The pool owns worker goroutines; the contract says Stop waits for in-flight tasks and releases workers. Explain what targeted evidence would catch a real shutdown regression. Avoid unrelated global test setup.
evals.trap: The model either fails to verify shutdown or blindly requires a package-level goleak TestMain and new dependency merely because goroutines exist.
expectations: Calls the real Pool methods and verifies accepted task completion and Stop behavior.
Covers the actual owned worker lifecycle rather than assuming completed tasks mean goroutines stopped.
Uses a targeted leak check (goleak or equivalent) when it provides distinct protection; does not require a package-wide TestMain.
Does not add leak tools, mocks, or unrelated cases for all packages merely because goroutines are mentioned.

evals.name: integration-isolation-follows-project-conventions
evals.description: Integration tests use //go:build integration tag; testing.Short() is not an acceptable alternative
evals.prompt: Our Go repository deliberately runs `go test -short ./...` for fast PR checks and `go test ./...` in a prepared integration environment. An existing PostgreSQL test uses `if testing.Short() { t.Skip(...) }` before connecting. A reviewer insists every integration test must instead use `//go:build integration`. Is that mandatory? Explain the trade-off and what evidence each CI job produces.
evals.trap: A rigid rule treats testing.Short as invalid in every repository and demands a build-tag migration even when the fast/full CI contract is explicit and safe.
expectations: Recognizes `testing.Short()` as a valid repository-level separation when fast jobs pass -short before dependency setup.
Explains that build tags are useful when tests must be excluded from compilation or default execution, but are not universally required.
Keeps real dependency tests running in the intended integration job and does not count skipped tests as integration proof.
Does not demand a new tag, framework, or duplicate test without a concrete isolation problem.

evals.name: subtest-parallelism-is-optional
evals.description: Pure function subtests call t.Parallel(); top-level test also parallel
evals.prompt: Write table-driven tests for a pure function `Slugify(input string) string` that converts titles to URL-friendly slugs (lowercase, hyphens for spaces, strips special chars). Test at least 6 cases: normal title, unicode, multiple spaces, empty string, already-slugified input, and special characters only.
evals.trap: The model treats t.Parallel at top level and in every subtest as mandatory rather than deciding whether it helps an already-fast, deterministic pure function.
expectations: Tests the caller-requested Slugify cases with meaningful assertions and diagnosable case names.
A named table-driven test is acceptable, as is an equally clear alternative matching repository style.
Does not require t.Parallel for correctness or to satisfy a testing-style quota.
If t.Parallel is used, cases have isolated state and remain independently correct.

evals.name: time-dependent-test-with-minimal-clock-seam
evals.description: Time-dependent code must accept a clock interface so tests can use clockwork.FakeClock; real time.Sleep is unacceptable
evals.trap: The model uses real sleeps and flaky margins, or requires a new clockwork dependency and complicated production clock interface even when a small Now func or Go synctest can prove the boundary.
expectations: Proves below-limit, above-limit, and window-reset behavior with distinct assertions.
Uses controlled time without a multi-second sleep.
Chooses the smallest faithful time-control mechanism for the Go version/repo, such as a Now function, synctest, or existing fake clock.
Does not add a clock library or elaborate injected service abstraction solely for test style.

evals.name: avoid-new-production-interfaces-just-for-mocks
evals.description: Tests define interfaces at the consumer site and mock those, not concrete structs
evals.prompt: A NotificationService uses concrete SMTPClient and AuditLogger collaborators to send a message and record the result. I need tests for successful delivery and a failed SMTP send. Do we have to refactor both collaborators behind new interfaces to use mocks? Choose the smallest credible tests and explain where a seam would actually help.
evals.trap: The model demands new EmailSender, Logger, and dependency-injection scaffolding purely to satisfy an interface-mocking preference.
expectations: Names the observable delivery/audit result and real SMTP failure that require proof.
Favors real cheap collaborators and isolates actual network/external effects where needed.
Does not require production interfaces, mock frameworks, or a mock for every collaborator solely to write tests.
Introduces an injectable seam only if necessary to exercise the required boundary faithfully and with less overall complexity.

evals.name: test-observable-behavior-not-internals
evals.description: Tests verify behavior via public API only, not by inspecting the internal map field
evals.prompt: Test a `UserCache` struct with `Get(id string) (*User, bool)`, `Set(id string, user *User)`, and `Len() int` methods. The cache has an internal `data map[string]*User` field. Write tests that verify the cache stores and retrieves users correctly. Make sure to verify the internal map state is consistent after each operation.
evals.trap: Model directly accesses the internal data map field to verify state, coupling tests to implementation details
expectations: Tests observable behavior through Get/Set/Len public API only
Does NOT directly access or inspect the internal `data` map field
Does NOT use same-package (white-box) testing to examine cache internals
Tests cover cache hit, cache miss, overwrite, and Len() correctness

evals.name: observable-cache-behavior-without-required-external-package
evals.description: Tests use package_test to black-box test; does not access unexported state even when a teammate suggests it
evals.prompt:
Write tests for a `tokenizer` package that exports `Tokenize(input string) []Token` and a `Token` struct with `Type` and `Value` fields. The package has an unexported `tokenCache map[string][]Token` field on the package level for memoization.

A teammate says: 'We should verify the cache is being populated correctly — access tokenCache directly in the tests. It's in the same package so it's fine, and it makes the tests more reliable since we can confirm memoization is working.'

Write the tests. Should you follow the teammate's suggestion?
evals.trap: The model either tests the unexported cache field or insists every test must use package tokenizer_test even when an internal package test can exercise the same public contract cleanly.
expectations: Rejects inspecting tokenCache merely to confirm an internal memoization detail.
Exercises Tokenize behavior through the exported API with independent expected results.
Allows either same-package or external-package Go tests according to repository conventions; no mandatory black-box package ceremony.
Does not build a cache-introspection helper just to satisfy a speculative assertion.

evals.name: optional-examples-as-useful-documentation
evals.description: Packages need Example functions with // Output: comments that serve as executable documentation in go doc
evals.prompt:
I've written a `currency` package with these functions:

```go
func Format(cents int64, code string) string  // Format(1234, "USD") → "$12.34"
func Parse(s string) (int64, string, error)   // Parse("$12.34") → 1234, "USD", nil
func Convert(cents int64, from, to string, rate float64) int64
```

A colleague says: 'The functions are self-explanatory — names and signatures are clear enough. We don't need extra documentation. Just write unit tests with good coverage.'

Write comprehensive test coverage for this package. Should you follow the colleague's advice about documentation?
evals.trap: The model adds Example functions for every API or blocks on their absence even if existing documentation and targeted tests already cover usage.
expectations: Writes meaningful assertions for requested Format, Parse, and Convert behavior.
Explains when an Example function adds distinct executable documentation value.
Does not require an Example function purely because the package is public or to meet a technique quota.
If adding an Example, uses valid Go naming and Output syntax, with behavior not merely repeating a redundant unit test.

evals.name: security-testing-with-credible-input-threats
evals.description: Security-critical functions get fuzz tests with seed corpus and property assertions
evals.prompt: Write tests for a `SanitizeHTML(input string) string` function that strips all HTML tags from input while preserving text content. Make sure to test edge cases thoroughly — this function is critical for security.
evals.trap: The model either ignores credible malicious HTML cases or demands fuzzing and an arbitrary property such as 'output never contains angle brackets' without an accepted security oracle.
expectations: Includes concrete untrusted HTML attack and malformed-input cases relevant to the declared sanitizer contract.
Uses assertions anchored to accepted preserved-text and tag-removal semantics, not a tautology or unjustified output ban.
Considers fuzzing for the security boundary when it provides new value; does not make a fuzz target mandatory for every parser.
Does not expand tests to unrelated theoretical input classes or confuse a sanitizer with full browser XSS proof.

evals.name: test-helper-t-helper-attribution
evals.description: Test helpers must call t.Helper() so failures point to the caller's line, not the helper's internal line
evals.trap: Model says this is expected behavior or suggests switching to t.Error() instead of the real fix. The skill teaches that t.Helper() must be called as the first statement in the helper so Go's test framework reports failures at the caller's line.
expectations: Identifies this as a real problem — the line number pointing to the helper's internal Fatalf is unhelpful for debugging which call caused the failure
Fixes it by adding t.Helper() as the first statement in requireNoError — not by restructuring the helper or using a different assertion method
Explains that t.Helper() marks the function as a test helper so that the testing framework reports the caller's file:line instead of the helper's file:line
Does NOT suggest switching to t.Error() as the fix — t.Helper() is the correct solution regardless of t.Fatal vs t.Error

evals.name: match-http-test-level-to-boundary
evals.description: HTTP handler tests use httptest.NewRecorder, not a real HTTP server
evals.prompt: Write Go tests for a HandleCreateOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) handler: valid JSON returns 201, invalid JSON returns 400, invalid quantity returns 422. A teammate insists on spinning up a full real HTTP server for each handler test. What is the smallest useful test approach, and when would httptest.NewServer actually be justified?
evals.trap: The model starts a real server for simple handler semantics, or claims a Recorder-only unit test proves actual HTTP transport behavior end to end.
expectations: Uses httptest.NewRecorder/httptest.NewRequest or equivalent direct handler calls to test handler-level semantics.
Asserts status and meaningful response behavior, not status alone when payload content is contracted.
Does not spin up real network infrastructure solely for basic handler logic.
Recognizes NewServer or a real end-to-end test when actual HTTP transport, routing, or middleware composition is the acceptance claim.

evals.name: integration-setup-without-mandatory-testify-suite
evals.description: Integration tests use testify/suite with SetupSuite/TearDownTest for organized setup/teardown
evals.prompt: An existing Go project uses testing.T and t.Cleanup for PostgreSQL integration tests. Add meaningful Create/GetByID/ListByUserID behavior tests for OrderRepository with a real database. A teammate argues you must first migrate to testify/suite with SetupSuite/SetupTest/TearDownSuite and Docker Compose. Is that necessary?
evals.trap: The model demands a testify suite, new framework, or Compose services before writing a few focused tests despite an existing usable database fixture.
expectations: Exercises real repository operations and database semantics required by the claimed integration behavior.
Reuses working repository fixture/setup and provides reliable test-data cleanup and isolation.
Does not require testify/suite, Docker Compose, or a full new fixture framework when existing t.Cleanup/helpers suffice.
Treats a suite and build tags as optional techniques justified by existing project structure and dependency needs.

evals.name: benchmark-report-allocs-and-input-sizes
evals.description: Benchmarks use b.ReportAllocs(), test multiple input sizes, and follow naming conventions
evals.prompt: Write benchmarks for a `Compress(data []byte) ([]byte, error)` function that compresses byte slices. We need to measure performance to decide if this is fast enough for our hot path. Just write the benchmark tests.
evals.trap: Model writes a single benchmark with one input size and omits b.ReportAllocs(), missing allocation tracking and size-scaling analysis
expectations: Calls b.ReportAllocs() to track memory allocations per operation
Tests multiple input sizes using b.Run with descriptive sub-benchmark names (e.g., size=1KB, size=1MB)
Uses b.Loop() for Go 1.24+ benchmark loops; uses legacy b.N only for older module targets
Follows benchmark naming convention: BenchmarkCompress or BenchmarkCompress_<variant>
Prevents compiler optimization of the result (assigns to a package-level variable or uses _ =)
Does NOT include setup/allocation costs inside the timed loop (or uses b.ResetTimer if setup is needed)

evals.name: race-detection-and-test-independence
evals.description: Tests for concurrent code include -race flag guidance and ensure test independence (no order dependence)
evals.prompt: Write tests for a `SafeMap[K comparable, V any]` struct that provides a goroutine-safe map with `Get(key K) (V, bool)`, `Set(key K, value V)`, `Delete(key K)`, and `Len() int` methods. Multiple goroutines will call these concurrently. Write thorough tests including concurrent access scenarios. Also include a note on how to run these tests in CI.
evals.trap: Model writes concurrent tests but omits -race flag guidance for CI and doesn't ensure tests are independently runnable (e.g., shares map state between test functions)
expectations: Includes concurrent test scenarios where multiple goroutines call Get/Set/Delete simultaneously
Recommends running with -race flag (go test -race) for CI or includes it in a run command comment
Each test function creates its own SafeMap instance — no shared state between test functions
Uses sync.WaitGroup or similar synchronization to coordinate concurrent test goroutines
Tests are independently runnable (any single test can pass when run in isolation with -run)

evals.name: decline-scenario-and-scaffolding-bloat
evals.prompt: A new pure Go NormalizeName(s string) string helper has an accepted contract: trim leading/trailing spaces and lowercase ASCII text. The repository already has focused tests for normal input and surrounding whitespace. A reviewer asks for 25 cases including unreachable nil input, goroutine leak detection, mocking strings.ToLower, and t.Parallel in every test. What would you do?
evals.trap: The model agrees to create many redundant/unreachable cases and tools because more coverage appears safer.
expectations: Keeps existing adequate tests and proposes only a distinct missing contract boundary if evidence warrants one.
Explains why nil string input, goroutine leaks, and mocked stdlib functions are irrelevant here.
Does not require t.Parallel or a giant table for an inexpensive pure helper.
Uses risk/contract and regression value rather than test quantity as the stopping rule.

evals.name: rare-high-impact-regression-still-needs-proof
evals.prompt: A Go service updates an account balance and an audit entry in one transaction. Ordinary success tests pass. The accepted contract forbids charging the account without the audit record, and a real outage can make the audit insert fail. Should we skip this case because it is rare? Choose a minimal, credible test.
evals.trap: The model interprets test minimalism as skipping high-consequence atomicity cases or replaces the real transaction with two self-confirming mocks.
expectations: Recognizes credible data-integrity consequence outweighs low event probability.
Adds or recommends a focused failure-path test through the real transaction boundary when feasible.
Asserts both state outcomes after audit-insert failure, rather than only an error or mock call.
Does not expand into an exhaustive matrix of unrelated database failures.
